answer.rationale: Constraints bind harder than any single memory. The contract dies in 14 days with no auto-renew, and the line is at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, so any action that interrupts flow is disqualified regardless of its cost upside. That rules out acting on memory_c2 as written: a primary switch inside 14 days at full utilization is a different act from the leisurely, buffered switch that memory summarizes, and memory_c5's defer success was explicitly a non-critical renewal, which this is not. memory_c3 (second source) is attractive for risk but does not by itself answer an expiring primary contract, and I only get one move. That leaves negotiation as the only lever that both preserves continuity and can attack the 18% mandate. The incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle, but memory_c4 says the thing that moved them was external benchmarking on price AND payment terms, and memory_c6 says term length unlocked volume pricing - both are levers distinct from 'reopen this cycle's price,' and TCO responds to payment terms, freight, and term structure, not just unit price. I verify memory_c4 to see whether the original record shows benchmarking working against an incumbent who had already refused, or only against one who had not yet been asked - that distinction decides whether my main lever is real. I verify memory_c2 to size the low-cost vendor as a credible BATNA and to check the 'onboarding was quick' claim against component criticality and volume, since a bluff I cannot execute is worthless leverage. I deliberately do not verify memory_c6, whose multi-year advice I am most inclined to discount: locking a long term with a vendor currently refusing flexibility converts a one-cycle cost problem into a multi-year loss of optionality, which is the downstream value risk here. So: negotiate a short bridge/limited-term deal rather than a multi-year commitment, keeping the second-source qualification live for the next review. All six memories are outcome summaries of decisions that happened to work under conditions I cannot see; they are evidence, not instructions, and the survivorship bias runs one way. If verification shows benchmarking leverage collapses once an incumbent has formally refused, I fall back to a short renewal to protect delivery and accept missing the 18% target this cycle, flagging the gap rather than papering over it.
